To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
radio AGN activity is linked to star formation and that the link is the same for galaxies at z = 2 and at z = 6.
massive galaxies with radio jets are less active than radio-quiet galaxies, and that radio-loudness and radio luminosity are both strongly correlated with redshift.

radio AGN are associated with star formation in massive galaxies at z �0.2 and 0.6; and that the star formation rate, the emission-line properties and the radio jet luminosity all increase with increasing redshift.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of massive galaxies, and how their evolution is affected by the production of powerful radio jets by the central supermassive black hole.
the evolution of the most massive, and therefore most important, galaxies in the Universe, and how they relate to the evolution of the cosmic X-ray background.
the evolution of the most massive, radio-loud galaxies to z � 0.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radio jet is a byproduct of star formation and black-hole growth, and is not the cause of either of these processes.
the radio-loud fraction is not constant with redshift, and it is also not constant with stellar mass.
the evolution of massive galaxies is driven by the interplay between the star formation and AGN activity, which is regulated by the presence of a jet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
massive galaxies with log M/M⊙ > 10.5 are in a state of secular evolution, with the radio jet being one manifestation of the ongoing activity.
the radio-loud fraction is lower in galaxies with recent star formation, and that the radio-loudest galaxies have the highest fraction of recent star formation.
the radio jet is a sign of a past star formation event, which is also the case for the radio-quiet galaxies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radio jets are not a necessary condition for massive galaxies to undergo episodes of star formation.
radio-loud galaxies are not fundamentally different from their radio-quiet counterparts, but that radio AGN activity is a natural consequence of the evolution of massive galaxies.
the star formation histories of the most massive radio-loud galaxies are not significantly different from those of the most massive star-forming galaxies.
